title: Lead me on
hookLine: the Handbook ends with old lines: Cleanthes asking to be led willingly, Socrates saying they can kill but not harm him (Enchiridion 52–53)

lines: THE HANDBOOK ENDS WITH OLD LINES.
A FOLDED NOTE IN A WALLET.
cards: Most books end with a summary. The handbook ends with a pocketful of old lines: not Epictetus' own words, but sayings from a poet, a hymn writer and Socrates, the way some people keep a folded note in a wallet.
Before he hands them over, there's one last short lesson about why people know so much and do so little. Then four sayings, to be kept at hand, he says, always. The handbook was made to be carried.
These are what he wanted carried last.

teach.h: USE FIRST, THEN PROOF, THEN LOGIC.
teach.b: Section fifty-two says philosophy has three parts. The first and most necessary is using the principles: for example, don't lie. The second is the proof: why one shouldn't lie.
The third checks the proofs: what makes a proof, what's true, what's false. The third exists for the second, and the second for the first. But people do the reverse, he says.
They spend their time on the third, and so they lie, while perfectly ready to prove that lying is wrong. Then the last section.

The first saying is by Cleanthes, the school's second head: Lead me, Zeus, and you, Destiny, wherever you've set me. I'll follow without hesitating. And if I'm unwilling, and turn bad, I'll follow all the same.
Seneca put these lines into Latin, and his version ends: the fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling.

teach.h: EURIPIDES AND CRITO: SO BE IT.
teach.b: From the poet Euripides: whoever yields well to necessity is wise among us, and knows the things of the gods. From Socrates, in prison, to his friend Crito: if this pleases the gods, so be it.

teach.h: THEY CAN KILL ME, NOT HARM ME.
teach.b: And the book's last line, Socrates again, at his trial: Anytus and Meletus, his accusers, can kill me, but they cannot harm me.
The handbook stops there. Not with an argument, but with a man who knew which part of him was out of anyone's reach.
Whether or not you share their picture of Zeus and destiny, the question stays: when the road goes where you didn't choose, will you walk it, or be dragged?

how: Some people practicing Stoicism memorize a few short lines, such as the closing sayings of the Enchiridion, and repeat them in hard moments.

the school head whose hymn says: lead me, and I'll follow

the most necessary part is using the principles, like not lying.

games.q: you can explain exactly why lying is wrong, with proofs. what does Enchiridion 52 say about you?
o: you've mastered the most important part.
you may still be lying, while ready to prove you shouldn't.
you should study the logic further.
games.why: we do the reverse, he says: we spend our time on proofs, and so we lie, while ready to show why lying is wrong.

practice: Let one of the four sayings stay with you: lead me on; yield well to what must be; if it pleases the gods, so be it; they can kill me, but not harm me.

Or, if none of these is yours, another old line that has steadied you, from scripture, a poem, or a person you loved. Say it quietly, once, then again, slower, and let it settle like a stone in a pocket.

wordCard.voice: Cleanthes. Author of the hymn that opens the handbook's last section: lead me, and I'll follow willingly. The fates lead the willing and drag the unwilling. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca's Letter 107: the fates lead the willing, and drag the unwilling.

carryVoice: Your line: willingly. The road is the same either way; the walking is yours. Onward, day three hundred eighty-six.
